title: Beyond the Lesson Plan: What Intentional Lesson Preparation Looks Like in Action
author: Teach Like a Champion
summary: This Teach Like a Champion post, built on reflections from Sadie McCleary, distinguishes lesson planning (what content to teach) from lesson preparation (a deliberate series of decisions about how to teach it). It names four preparation practices: planning the exemplar response, planning for error with Back Pocket Questions, planning for active observation, and planning the means of participation. The post then shows these in action through a second-grade ELA lesson in Carlsbad, New Mexico, where teacher Danielle Dahl annotates her exemplar in the text, flags a Point of Difficulty around the word because, and plans two observation laps with specific targets. She also writes her preparation on the same handout students use so she can compare their work with her exemplar at a glance. The argument is that preparation makes teachers agile rather than rigid, freeing attention to respond to students in real time.
points: Lesson planning decides what content to teach, whereas lesson preparation decides how to teach it, including the specific moves and checks.
Four practices anchor preparation: drafting the exemplar response, anticipating errors with Back Pocket Questions, deciding what student data to gather, and scripting participation.
Flagging Points of Difficulty in advance, such as students citing evidence without explaining why it matters, tells the teacher exactly what to watch for.
Planned observation laps give circulation a target, producing real-time data on whose work to show and how to review.
Writing preparation onto the student handout lets the teacher compare exemplar and student work without splitting attention.
quotes: While most educators are familiar with lesson plans - what content will be taught, often mapped to a curriculum or instructional framework - Lesson Preparation is a distinct process. It is about making a deliberate series of decisions regarding how to teach that plan.
Those questions matter because great teaching isn’t just about knowing the content, it’s about anticipating the moments where students will think, struggle, and grow.

Planning for Error: Anticipating common gaps or misconceptions and preparing responses ahead of time using Back Pocket Questions (BPQs). Planning for Active Observation: Deciding in advance what student data you will gather during the lesson and how you will collect it.
Knowing students often pull accurate quotes without explaining why they matter, she primed herself to watch closely for whether students connected their evidence to its purpose.

Rather than circulating without a target, Danielle planned specific rounds of data collection. On Lap 1, she checked for an accurate answer to Question 1 paired with text evidence, and her class crushed it.

Subtle but important, Danielle wrote her preparation directly onto the exact same handout students used in class. By matching formats, she can glance between her own exemplar and student work without splitting her attention.

When teachers invest time in Lesson Preparation, anticipating errors, scripting participation, and deciding what data to look for, they free up their attention in the classroom to respond to students in real time. Preparation does not make teaching rigid. It makes teachers agile.
context: The post separates what a lesson plan covers from the extra decisions that make delivery effective.
It ties good teaching to anticipating where students will struggle, which motivates preparing beyond the plan.
Two of the four practices target errors and observation, so the teacher knows what to look for and say.
The example shows how a flagged Point of Difficulty directs the teacher's attention during the lesson.
Observation laps give circulating a defined purpose and produce usable evidence of understanding.
A small format choice, using the student handout, reduces the teacher's cognitive load in the room.
The closing claim is that preparation frees attention and makes teaching more responsive, not more scripted.
